q: Your browser opens example.org. What does DNS do in that moment?
choices: It gives the address that goes with the name
It sends the page to your browser
It encrypts the connection
It picks the fastest cable
explain: DNS is a phone book: you give it a name, it gives back an IP address. Then your browser connects to that address itself; DNS doesn't carry the page. So when only names fail and addresses still work, the network is fine and DNS is the problem.

q: One server runs a website and SSH. How does a client say which of the two it wants?
choices: With the port number
With a different IP address for each
With the server's name
With its own MAC address
explain: The address finds the machine; the port picks the service on it, like a door number in a building. SSH usually listens on 22, HTTPS on 443. A service can be set to another port, so when a connection fails, check which port the service really listens on.

q: A site won't open. Which question do you ask first?
choices: Does the name give an address?
Is the page's HTML valid?
Is the server's disk full?
Which browser is it?
explain: Follow the order of the trip: the name must give an address, the address must answer, the port must accept, then the service answers. Each step needs the one before. Checking the name first rules out DNS in seconds, before you blame the server or the page.

q: ping to the server works, but the connection to its port is refused. Which layer do you look at?
choices: 4, transport: nothing listens on that port
1, physical: the cable
3, network: the route
2, link: the MAC address
explain: ping answered, so cable, link and route work (layers 1 to 3). Refused means the machine itself said no: no program listens on that port, or it listens on another address. Check that the service runs, on which port and address, before touching the network.

q: ping gets no answer from a server. What can you conclude?
choices: Not much: a firewall may block ping
The server is off
The cable is cut
DNS is broken
explain: ping uses ICMP, and many firewalls drop it on purpose. No answer can mean the machine is off, the route is missing, or ICMP is blocked. Try a test higher up: if a web page or an SSH connection works, the machine is clearly up.

q: The page loads, but shows "500 Internal Server Error". Where is the problem?
choices: In the application on the server
In the cable
In DNS
In your Wi-Fi
explain: To get any HTTP answer, the name, the route and the connection all had to work. 500 is the application saying it failed while handling your request. Look at the application's logs on the server, not at the network.

q: On your local network, what does ARP find out?
choices: Which network card (MAC) has a given IP
Which name goes with an IP
Which port a service uses
Which route leads to the Internet
explain: Inside a local network, frames are addressed to a network card by its MAC address. ARP asks everyone "who has this IP?" and the owner answers with its MAC. The machine keeps answers in a cache: ip neigh on Linux, arp -a on a Mac. Names are DNS's job, not ARP's.

q: You send data to a server on the Internet. Whose MAC address is on the frame that leaves your machine?
choices: Your router's (the gateway)
The far server's
Your DNS server's
Nobody's: the Internet has no MAC
explain: A MAC address only counts on your own network. For a far machine, your computer sends the frame to the gateway's MAC; the IP packet inside keeps the far address. Each router then passes it to its next neighbour. That's why a gateway that doesn't answer ARP cuts you off from everything outside.

q: ping uses ICMP. Which port does it test?
choices: None: ICMP has no ports
Port 80
Port 22
The port of the last service used
explain: ICMP travels inside IP, at the network layer, and has no ports: ping only tells you the machine answers, not that a service works. A web server can be down while ping succeeds, and ping can fail while the web server works. To test a service, connect to its port: curl for a website, ssh for SSH.

q: A video call drops a few packets now and then. Why does it use UDP rather than TCP?
choices: Late sound is useless: better skip it than wait
UDP is encrypted, TCP isn't
UDP never loses packets
TCP can't carry sound
explain: TCP resends what's lost and waits to deliver in order: perfect for a file, bad for live sound, where a resent piece arrives too late to play. UDP just sends, and the program hides small losses. That's also why most DNS queries use UDP: one short question, asked again if no answer comes.

q: A firewall rule opens port 53 for TCP. DNS queries to the server still fail. Why?
choices: DNS queries mostly use UDP: open UDP 53 too
Port 53 is reserved for the firewall
DNS needs port 80
The rule needs a reboot
explain: TCP port 53 and UDP port 53 are two different doors. Most DNS queries travel over UDP; TCP is used for big answers and zone transfers. Open the protocol the service really uses: ss -tuln on a Linux server shows udp and tcp lines separately.

q: How do you check that a DNS server answers on UDP?
choices: Ask it a real query: dig @server example.org
ping its port 53
Wait for a refused message
Open it in a browser
explain: UDP has no connection, so there's nothing to "connect" to: a closed port may answer with an ICMP error, a filtered one stays silent, so silence proves nothing. The sure test is a real question the service must answer, here a DNS query sent to that server. ping can't help: it has no port.

q: What is the difference between broadcast and multicast?
choices: Broadcast reaches everyone nearby, multicast only a group
Multicast is only for IPv4
Broadcast crosses routers, multicast doesn't
They are two names for the same thing
explain: Broadcast goes to every machine of the local network: ARP uses it to ask who has an IP. Multicast goes to a group address, and only the machines that joined that group listen. IPv6 dropped broadcast entirely and uses multicast instead.

q: A colleague finds printer.local from one office, but not from another subnet. Why?
choices: mDNS multicast doesn't cross routers
The printer blocks that office
printer.local is a public name
The other subnet uses IPv6
explain: Names ending in .local are answered by mDNS, sent to 224.0.0.251, an address routers never forward. So the printer is only found by name inside its own network. Add it by its IP address, or ask the network team for an mDNS relay between the two networks.

q: Which of these addresses is a multicast group?
explain: Multicast addresses are 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 (224.0.0.0/4); 224.0.0.251 is the group mDNS uses. 192.168.1.255 is the broadcast address of a /24 network, 127.0.0.1 the machine itself, 10.0.0.1 an ordinary private address.

q: A download page shows a SHA-256 next to the file. Yours matches. What does that prove?
choices: The file arrived unchanged
The file has no virus
The file comes from the vendor
The file is encrypted
explain: A hash is a fingerprint: the same bytes always give the same one, and one changed bit gives a completely different one. A match proves your copy equals the one the page describes. It says nothing about who made it: someone who changed the file could change the page too. That's what signatures are for.

q: You want to send Sam a file only Sam can open. Which key locks it?
choices: Sam's public key
Your private key
Sam's private key
Your public key
explain: What a public key locks, only the matching private key opens. Sam gives the public key to anyone (check its fingerprint with Sam); the private key never leaves Sam. Your own private key is for signing, not for locking a file for someone else.

q: Your system checks an update's signature before installing it. What does a good signature tell you?
choices: It comes from that key's owner, unchanged
That nobody else can read it
That it has no bugs
That it is the newest version
explain: Only the holder of the private key can sign; anyone with the public key can check. A good signature proves the update comes from that key's owner and wasn't changed since. It hides nothing: updates aren't secret. Your system trusts the vendor's key because it came with the system. It doesn't prove the code is good.

q: Why does a web server run as its own user, like www-data, rather than root?
choices: If it's broken into, the damage stays small
root is slower
It's required by HTTP
So it can read everyone's files
explain: A program has the rights of the user it runs as. Run as root, a flaw in the web server gives the attacker the whole machine. As www-data, they only reach what www-data may touch. One user per service keeps each breach small: that's least privilege. (Only a small starter process keeps root, to open port 80.)

q: Opening a file says "Permission denied". What does it tell you?
choices: Your user lacks the right on it
The file is damaged
The disk is full
The file doesn't exist
explain: Every access is checked against the file's owner, group and rights. Denied means that check said no for your user, on the file or on a folder on the way to it. Look at who owns it and which rights each kind of person has before reaching for sudo. A missing file says "No such file or directory" instead.

q: Three teammates must all edit the same folder. What's the clean way?
choices: A group with the three, given write on it
Open it to everyone
Share one login between them
Run everything as root
explain: Rights go to an owner, a group and everyone else. Put the three in one group and give that group write: each keeps their own login, and a newcomer just joins the group. Also set the folder's setgid bit (chmod g+s) so new files take the group. Opening to everyone lets any user change the files.

q: You start the same script in two terminals. How many processes run it?
choices: Two, each with its own PID
One, shared
None: a script isn't a process
As many as the script has lines
explain: A program or script on disk is just a file. Each time you start it, the system makes a new process with its own memory and number, the PID. Two starts, two processes: stopping one leaves the other running.

q: What makes a service (a daemon) different from a command you type?
choices: It runs with no terminal, often from boot
It is always written in C
It can't be stopped
It runs only while you're logged in
explain: A command you type belongs to your terminal and usually ends with it. A service is a process with no terminal that waits for work: a web server, SSH, a database. On most Linux systems, systemd starts it at boot, can restart it if it crashes, and keeps its logs.

q: A program is stuck. What do you try first?
choices: Ask it to stop, then force only if needed
Force it at once
Unplug the machine
Delete its program file
explain: Asked to stop, a program can finish writing its files and clean up. Forced, it stops mid-way: half-written files, lock files left behind. Ask first, wait a few seconds, and force only when it won't stop. The Processes lesson shows how: kill (a polite TERM), then kill -9 (KILL, the force).

q: A script compares each of n customers with each of n subscribers. The lists grow 10 times. The work?
choices: About 100 times more
About 10 times more
The same
About 20 times more
explain: A loop inside a loop does n × n comparisons. Ten times more on each side gives 10 × 10 = 100 times more work. That's why a script fine on a sample can take hours on the real data: count how the work grows before the data does.

q: A script runs in a second on a 100-line sample. The real file has a million lines. What do you check first?
choices: How its work grows with the number of lines
Whether the disk is fast enough
Whether the file is in UTF-8
Nothing: one second is fast
explain: Speed on 100 lines says nothing about a million. Work that grows like n gets 10 000 times longer; like n × n, 100 million times. Look for a loop inside a loop, or measure on 100 then 200 lines: time × 2 is fine, time × 4 is trouble.

q: Why is finding a word in a paper dictionary fast, even with 100 000 words?
choices: Sorted: each look throws away half the rest
You read every page quickly
The words are short
The first letter is enough
explain: Because the words are sorted, you open in the middle and keep only the half where the word must be. 100 000 words take about 17 looks, a million about 20: that's log n. Databases use the same idea with indexes.

q: You mistype one digit of your card number and the form says "invalid" at once. How does it know?
choices: The last digit is a check computed from the others
It asked your bank
It knows every card number
It guessed from the card's color
explain: Card numbers end with a check digit computed with the Luhn formula. One wrong digit, or most swaps of two neighbours, breaks the check, so the form knows without asking anyone. It can't tell which digit is wrong: it detects, it doesn't correct.

q: A QR code with a scratch across part of it still scans. Why?
choices: It carries extra data that rebuilds the missing part
The phone guesses the link
The scratched part held nothing
QR codes are stored online
explain: QR codes add error-correcting data (Reed–Solomon codes) computed from the content. Depending on the level chosen, about 7% to 30% can be lost and rebuilt. That's why a logo can sit in the middle. But scratch one of the three big corner squares, which tell the phone where the code is, and it may not scan.

q: A downloaded file doesn't match its published checksum. What do you do?
choices: Download it again: a checksum detects, it can't repair
Fix the bytes by hand
Use it anyway if it opens
Change the checksum to match
explain: A checksum like SHA-256 finds that something changed, not what. The copy is damaged or not the right file: download it again, ideally from the official site. If it still doesn't match, don't use it: someone may have changed it.

q: What does a git commit hold?
choices: A snapshot of the project, with author, date and why
Only the lines you typed today
A backup of your whole disk
The list of your branches
explain: A commit saves the state of the whole project at that moment, with who made it, when, and a message saying why. Commits chain together into the history. You can go back to any of them, compare two, or find the one that broke something.

q: You want to try a risky idea without breaking the code that works. What do you use in git?
choices: A branch
A copy of the folder named _old
A new repository
A commit with no message
explain: A branch is a line of work beside the main one: your commits go on it and main doesn't move. If the idea works, you merge it; if not, you delete the branch and main never saw it. Copying folders by hand is what git saves you from.

q: You committed a password, then deleted it in the next commit. Is it safe now?
choices: No: it stays in the history; change the password
Yes, the file no longer has it
Yes, if nobody pushed for an hour
Yes, git hides deleted lines
explain: git keeps every commit, so the old version with the password is still there for anyone with the repository. Treat the secret as leaked: change it first. Then keep secrets out of the repository for good, for example in a file git ignores. Ignoring a file that is already committed changes nothing: git rm --cached stops tracking it.

q: You need every line of a log that holds a date, whatever the date. What fits?
choices: A regular expression describing a date's shape
Searching for today's date
Reading the log by eye
Sorting the log
explain: You don't know the exact text, only its shape: four digits, a dash, two digits, a dash, two digits. A regular expression describes that shape, and grep -E finds every line that matches. Plain text search only finds one exact date.

q: You search prices for 1.5 with a regex. Lines with 105 show up too. Why?
choices: In a regex, . means any character
grep ignores dots
105 and 1.5 are the same number
The file is broken
explain: A few characters are special in a regex, and the dot matches any single character, so 1.5 also matches 105 or 1x5. For an exact text, search plain text (grep -F '1.5') or escape the dot inside single quotes (grep '1\.5').

q: You need one field from a JSON file. Regex or a JSON tool?
choices: A JSON tool like jq: a regex breaks on nesting
A regex: it's always faster
A regex, if the file is small
Neither: open it and copy by hand
explain: JSON can nest, spread over lines, escape quotes and change order: a regex that works today breaks on the next file. A parser understands the format: jq, or Python's json module. Keep regexes for shapes in plain lines.

q: Two programs append to the same CSV file at once and lines get mixed. What does a database add?
choices: Safe writes from many programs, one at a time
Prettier columns
A smaller file
Nothing: it's the same
explain: A text file has no rules for two writers: their lines can interleave or cut each other. A database takes the writes one at a time, checks them, and keeps each change whole. For one program writing small data, a CSV is fine.

q: In a customers table, what is one row?
choices: One customer
One detail, like every email
The whole table
The list of columns
explain: Like a spreadsheet: each row is one thing, here one customer, and each column one detail about it (name, email, city). A column holds the same detail for every customer.

q: A phone app keeps its data in one file inside the app, with no server. What does it likely use?
choices: SQLite
PostgreSQL
A CSV per row
An Excel sheet
explain: SQLite is a database in a single file, run inside the program itself: phones, browsers and many small tools use it. PostgreSQL and MySQL are servers that many programs reach over the network, for data many machines share, like a busy website's.

q: What does a compiler like gcc do?
choices: Translates source code once into a program the CPU runs
Runs your code line by line, each time
Checks your spelling in comments
Downloads libraries
explain: A CPU only understands machine code. A compiler reads your source code and writes a program file of machine code, once; then that file runs on its own. An interpreter, like python3, reads your code and runs it each time instead.

q: A Python script misspells a variable name (totl instead of total) in a branch that rarely runs. When will you find out?
choices: Only when that line runs
When you save the file
When Python is installed
Never: Python fixes typos
explain: Before it starts, Python checks the grammar of the whole file, so a syntax error stops it at once. But a name is only looked up when its line runs: a misspelled name in a branch that never ran stays hidden, and can blow up months later. Test every branch; in C or Rust the compiler would have refused to build.

q: You compiled a C program on Linux x86_64. Will that file run on a Mac with an arm64 chip?
choices: No: build it again for that system
Yes, machine code is the same everywhere
Yes, if you rename it
Only with sudo
explain: A compiled program holds machine code for one kind of CPU and one system. A Mac with an arm64 chip needs a program built for macOS on arm64: compile the source again there. A Python script, by contrast, runs wherever python3 and the libraries it uses are installed.

q: Why learn the OSI layers if the Internet runs on TCP/IP?
choices: To sort a failure by where it happens
Because routers use all 7 layers
Because exams are the only use
Because TCP/IP has 7 layers too
explain: OSI is a model for reasoning: physical, link, network, transport, application. TCP/IP merges some of them (5 and 6 are blurry), but the order still holds: each layer needs the one below. Saying "layer 4" or "it's DNS" turns "the network is down" into a place to look.

q: A TCP connection fails at once with "Connection refused". What does that tell you?
choices: The machine answered: no program listens on that port
A firewall silently dropped it
The name doesn't resolve
The cable is unplugged
explain: Refused is an answer: the machine is up and reachable, and its system replied that nothing listens there (rarely, a firewall set to reject, not drop). A firewall that drops packets gives a time out instead, after a long wait. So refused sends you to the service (is it running, on which address and port?), not to the network.

q: A script stores a password "encrypted" with base64. Is it protected?
choices: No: base64 is an encoding, anyone decodes it
Yes, base64 is strong encryption
Yes, if the file ends in .b64
Only if the password is long
explain: base64 only rewrites bytes as letters so they travel in text: base64 -d turns it back, no key needed. It's not encryption and not a hash. Keep the secret out of the script: a secret store, a file only that service's user can read (mode 600), or systemd's LoadCredential=. Not Environment=: any user can read it.

q: An install fails without root. What's the good habit?
choices: sudo for that one command
Log in as root for the day
Give your user every right
Open the folder to everyone
explain: sudo runs one command as root and then you're yourself again, and the system logs who ran what. Staying root all day turns every typo into a possible disaster, for the whole machine. Least privilege: root only for the command that needs it.

q: You close your terminal: your script stops, but the web server keeps running. Why?
choices: The script was tied to your terminal; the server isn't
The server is faster
Scripts can't run for long
The web server runs as you
explain: Closing the terminal sends a hang-up signal to everything started from it, and your script stops on it. The web server was started by systemd, not by you, and has no terminal to lose. That's why long-running work belongs in a service.

q: A script takes 1 s on 1 000 lines and 4 s on 2 000. How does its work grow?
choices: Like n × n: look for a loop inside a loop
Like n: it's fine
It doesn't grow
Like log n
explain: Twice the data and four times the time is the sign of n × n: at 20 000 lines, expect about 400 s. Work growing like n would only double. Look for a loop inside a loop, or a command that reads a whole file for each line.

q: Why can't a card's check digit correct the typo it found?
choices: One digit only says something is wrong, not where
Banks forbid it
It could, but forms don't bother
It only works on the first digit
explain: A single check digit carries just enough to notice a change. To find where the error is, and so fix it, a code needs more extra data, like the error-correcting part of a QR code. Detecting is enough here: you can simply type the number again.

q: Why does a commit message say why, not just what?
choices: The diff shows what; only the message keeps the why
git refuses short messages
It makes the commit smaller
So the branch gets a name
explain: Anyone can see what changed by comparing versions. Why it changed lives only in the message: the bug it fixes, the decision behind it. Months later, it's what tells you whether a strange line is safe to remove.

q: An AI gives you a regex for your logs. How do you trust it?
choices: Test it on lines that must match and lines that must not
If it's long, it's right
Run it once on production
Ask the AI if it's sure
explain: A regex can match too much or too little, and both look fine at a glance. Gather a few real lines that should match and a few that shouldn't, and check each. Keep them: they become a test when the regex changes.

q: A transfer debits one account, then the server crashes before crediting the other. What prevents a half-done transfer?
choices: A transaction: all its changes, or none
A backup every night
A faster server
Writing to a CSV
explain: A transaction groups the debit and the credit: the database applies both, or, after a crash, neither. Nobody ever sees money that left one account and reached no other. A nightly backup would lose the day and not fix the half-done change.

q: On a new server, python3 app.py says "python3: command not found". Why?
choices: A script needs its interpreter installed there
The script has a typo
Python only runs on laptops
The server is out of disk
explain: A Python script isn't a program on its own: python3 reads it and runs it. Install python3 on that server, and the libraries the script needs (in a venv). A compiled program wouldn't need an interpreter, but it must be built for that server's system.

q: Why can grep read the output of ls, of ps, or a log file, all the same way?
choices: They all write lines of text
grep knows every program's format
They were written by the same people
grep only works on log files
explain: On Unix almost everything is text: logs, configuration files, and what commands print. A tool that reads lines can read the output of almost any other tool, which is why small tools chain so well.

q: No command tells you which address sends your server the most requests. What's the Unix way to get it?
choices: Install a big log analysis suite first
Read the log by hand and count
Chain small tools with pipes: cut, sort, uniq -c, sort
Ask the server to log less
explain: Unix tools each do one small job. One takes the address out of each line, one groups equal lines, one counts them, one sorts the counts: chained with pipes, they answer a question none of them answers alone.

q: In cmd1 | cmd2, what goes through the pipe?
choices: Everything cmd1 shows, errors included
What cmd1 prints on its standard output, as cmd2's input
A copy of the files cmd1 opened
Only cmd1's exit code
explain: The pipe carries cmd1's standard output into cmd2's standard input. Error messages go to another stream, standard error, so by default they still show on your screen instead of going into cmd2 (2>&1 would send them in too).

q: Your pipe cuts a CSV file on commas. It goes wrong on lines where a field is "Paris, France" in quotes. What's the lesson?
choices: Pipes can't handle files over a few lines
Commas are not allowed in CSV files
Add more cut commands until it works
Text is loose: structured data needs a tool for its format
explain: Small tools see lines and separators, not the meaning of quotes. For simple lines they are fast and enough; for a format with rules (CSV with quoted fields, JSON), use a tool that reads that format, such as Python's csv module or jq for JSON.

q: Every Monday you run the same 10 commands, in order. Why put them in a script?
choices: Scripts run faster than commands typed by hand
Same steps every time, none forgotten, readable by others
A script can't make mistakes
Typed commands are not saved anywhere
explain: A script doesn't get tired: it runs the same steps in the same order every time. The steps live in a file, so a teammate can read, review and run them too. It can still contain a mistake, which is why you test it.

q: Which job fits bash better than Python?
choices: Archive a folder with tar and copy it away with rsync
Read a JSON reply and pick out nested fields
Compute averages over a large CSV file
A 500-line program with careful error handling
explain: Bash is made to run other programs and chain them: tar, rsync, cp. Working on structured data, computing, or a long program with careful error handling is Python's ground.

q: Your new script will rename 300 photos. What do you do first?
choices: Run it on all 300 at once: it's faster
Delete the originals to save room
Try it on a few copies, printing what it would do
Nothing: if it runs once, it's right
explain: A script repeats a mistake as fast as it repeats good work: a bug hits all 300 files. Try it on a copy or a few files first, and have it show what it would do before it does it.

q: Your bash script has grown to 400 lines, with arrays of arrays and JSON parsing. What does Google's shell style guide say to do?
choices: Split it into four 100-line bash files
Rewrite it in a more structured language, such as Python
Remove the comments to make it shorter
Nothing: bash has no size limit
explain: Google's shell style guide says that past about 100 lines, or once the control flow stops being simple, a script should be rewritten in a more structured language, early, because scripts grow. Python is the usual pick: it has nested data structures, a JSON parser and exceptions. Bash is great glue, but it has only flat arrays (no arrays of arrays) and no exceptions.

q: Why install nginx with apt or dnf instead of downloading it and copying its files yourself?
choices: It's the only way to run nginx on Linux
Packages are always the newest version
Files copied by hand can't be run
It handles its libraries, its updates and its removal
explain: A package manager fetches the libraries a program needs, records every file it puts on the disk, updates everything at once (security fixes included), and removes it cleanly later. Copy files by hand and all of that is your job.

q: How do apt and dnf know a package really comes from the repository?
choices: They check a signature with a key they already trust
They compare the file size with the website
The download uses HTTPS, so it must be right
They don't: they install whatever comes
explain: Everything comes signed: Debian signs the repository's list, which holds a checksum of each package; Rocky signs each package. apt and dnf check that signature with a key they already trust and refuse a package that doesn't match. HTTPS alone only protects the trip, not who made the file. That's also why adding a third-party repository means adding its key.

q: A README says: curl https://get.example.com | sudo bash. What's the problem?
choices: curl is too slow for big downloads
bash can't read scripts from a pipe
It runs a script you haven't read, as root
Nothing, it's the recommended way on Debian
explain: That line runs whatever the server sends, as root, before you can read it. What it installs may never be recorded (no updates, no clean removal), or it may add a repository you didn't choose. Look for your distribution's package first, or add the vendor's repository with its key.

q: An admin moves between a Debian server and a Rocky server. Which pair of package tool and package file matches each?
choices: Debian: dnf and .rpm; Rocky: apt and .deb
Debian: apt and .deb; Rocky: dnf and .rpm
Both use apt, only the package files differ
Both use dnf, only the package files differ
explain: Debian and Ubuntu use apt with .deb packages; Rocky, Alma and Red Hat use dnf with .rpm packages. The ideas are the same (signed repositories, dependencies, a local database), the commands and files differ.

q: A local variable of a C function: where does it live, and when does it go away?
choices: On the stack, gone when the function returns
On the heap, until you call free
On the disk, until the program ends
In a register, never freed
explain: Each function call gets a box on the stack for its local variables. When the function returns, the box is gone by itself: nothing to free. (A local marked static is the exception: it lives as long as the program.) That's also why you must never return the address of a local variable.

q: Your program reads a file and keeps every line. You learn how many lines there are only while it runs. Where does that data go?
choices: On the stack, it's faster
In the program file itself
In the CPU cache
On the heap, where the program asks for room as it needs it
explain: The stack is small, and a function's box disappears when it returns. Data that is big, or whose size you learn only while running, goes on the heap, and stays there until it's freed.

q: Who frees heap memory in C, in Python and in Rust?
choices: The operating system, every second, in all three
C: you (free); Python: itself; Rust: the value's owner
Nobody: heap memory is never freed
C: the compiler; Python: you; Rust: a garbage collector
explain: C trusts you to call free, once, at the right time. Python frees a value as soon as nothing uses it (it counts the uses); its garbage collector frees values that only point to each other. Rust frees a value when its one owner goes out of scope, and the compiler refuses code that uses it afterwards. Rust makes leaks rare, not impossible.

q: A server's memory grows a little every hour until the system kills it. What's the most likely cause?
choices: The stack is too small
The server's disk is full
A leak: memory taken on the heap and never given back
Too many local variables
explain: Stack memory comes back by itself when functions return, so it doesn't grow for days. Memory that grows slowly and never comes back is heap memory nobody frees: a leak. In C, AddressSanitizer (gcc -fsanitize=address) shows where it was taken: by default on Linux, with ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1 on a Mac. Valgrind does it too, on Linux only.

q: What does CI do when you push?
choices: It deploys your laptop's files to production
It reviews your code instead of a person
It merges every branch into main
A machine builds and tests it, the result is on the commit
explain: Continuous integration builds and tests every push automatically, on a fresh machine. The result, pass or fail, shows on the commit and on the pull request or merge request, minutes after the push, while a mistake is still small. People still review the code.

q: "It works on my laptop." How does CI help with that?
choices: It starts from a fresh machine: a forgotten dependency fails
It copies your laptop's setup to everyone
It runs the program faster
It hides the errors other people would see
explain: Your laptop has years of things installed. A hosted CI job starts from a fresh machine with the same known image every time, then installs what the project declares. A dependency that exists only on your laptop is missing there, so the job fails before a teammate or a server finds out. (A runner your team hosts itself may keep files between jobs: check how it is set up.)

q: Continuous delivery or continuous deployment: what's the difference?
choices: They are two names for the same thing
Delivery runs the tests, deployment doesn't
Delivery: a person presses go; deployment: it goes alone
Deployment is only for mobile apps
explain: Both build the release automatically once the tests pass. With continuous delivery, a person decides when it goes to production; with continuous deployment, every passing change goes out by itself.

q: Where does a GitLab project's pipeline live, and why does that matter?
choices: On GitLab's servers only, out of the team's hands
In .gitlab-ci.yml in the repository, reviewed like code
In each developer's home folder
In a database nobody can change
explain: The pipeline is a YAML file in the repository (.gitlab-ci.yml on GitLab, .github/workflows/ on GitHub). It changes through commits, with a history and a review. The deploy keys are not written in it (they live in the project's CI/CD settings), but its jobs can use them: whoever changes the file can make a job use them. Review a change to it as carefully as a change to the server.
